noteBlocks.md: Twenty-two of your pairs of chromosomes match. The twenty-third need not, and that pair decides whether a baby is a girl or a boy. The same Punnett squares you used for crosses explain how some conditions run in families, and why a test before birth can be a hard choice.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which pair is the odd one out here, and what does it tell you about whose chromosomes these are?

noteBlocks.md:
The first 22 pairs match. The **twenty-third pair** is the **sex chromosomes**, and it is the only pair that can be mismatched.

A **female** has two X chromosomes: **XX**.
A **male** has one X and one much shorter Y: **XY**.

noteBlocks.explain: Male. The short chromosome is a Y, and only a male has one.

noteBlocks.md:
Sperm are made by meiosis from **germ cells** in the testes. A germ cell holds an **X and a Y**. Meiosis puts **one** sex chromosome into each sperm, so half the sperm carry an **X** and half carry a **Y**.

Every egg carries an **X**, because a mother has only X chromosomes to give. So the sperm decides: an X sperm makes a girl, and a Y sperm makes a boy.

noteBlocks.prompt: An egg is fertilised by a sperm that carries a Y chromosome. Which sex chromosomes will the baby have?
noteBlocks.explain: XY. The egg always gives an X and this sperm gave the Y, so the baby is a boy.

noteBlocks.title: Worked example: draw the Punnett square for sex determination, and give the ratio of boys to girls it predicts. [4]
noteBlocks.md:
**Step 1 — the parents.** Mother **XX**, father **XY**. **[1]**
**Step 2 — the gametes.** Her eggs: X and X. His sperm: X and Y. **[1]**
**Step 3 — the square.** XX, XY, XX, XY. **[1]**
**Step 4 — the ratio.** 2 XY and 2 XX: **1 : 1** boys to girls, a **50%** chance either way. **[1]**

The square is the same for every pregnancy, so the children born before change nothing.

noteBlocks.prompt: A couple already have two daughters. What is the percentage chance that their next baby is a boy?
noteBlocks.explain: 50%. Half the sperm carry a Y every time; the earlier children make no difference.

noteBlocks.md:
**Cystic fibrosis** is caused by a **recessive** allele. A person needs **two** copies, so someone with one copy is a **carrier**: heterozygous, with no symptoms.

**Huntington's disease** is caused by a **dominant** allele. **One** copy is enough, so a person with it may be **homozygous dominant or heterozygous**.

**Down's syndrome** is not caused by an allele at all: there is an **extra copy of chromosome 21**.

noteBlocks.title: Both genotypes, not one
noteBlocks.md: Asked for every genotype that gives Huntington's disease, only a minority of candidates chose both. One copy of a dominant allele is enough, so the heterozygote has it too.

noteBlocks.prompt: A person has Huntington's disease. Which description fits their genotype?
noteBlocks.explain: Either. One copy of the dominant allele is enough, and two copies give it as well.

noteBlocks.title: What to let pass
noteBlocks.md: The video is made for another board. If it uses an example CCEA does not name, let it go by: CCEA's conditions are cystic fibrosis, Huntington's disease, Down's syndrome and, at Higher, haemophilia.

In the family shown, both parents are carriers, **Ff**. Each passes on **F** or **f**, so a child can be **FF**, **Ff** or **ff**.

One box in four is **ff**: a **25%** chance of a child with cystic fibrosis. Two boxes in four are **Ff**, carriers like their parents. That is how a recessive allele passes through a family unseen.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two carriers of cystic fibrosis are expecting a baby. Give the percentage chance that the baby is a carrier.
noteBlocks.explain: 50%. Two of the four boxes are Ff, with one allele of each kind.

noteBlocks.alt: A karyogram: the chromosomes of one person sorted into numbered groups, 1 to 22, and the sex chromosomes. Every numbered group holds two chromosomes except group 21, which holds 3. The last group holds one long X and one short Y. The whole set therefore holds 47 chromosomes instead of 46.
noteBlocks.caption: Every numbered group is a pair except group 21, which has three.

noteBlocks.md:
Down's syndrome begins with a gamete that carries one chromosome too many: an egg with **24** instead of **23**, for example. Fertilised by a sperm with **23**, it gives a cell with **47**.

Every cell of the baby is copied from that one by mitosis, so every body cell holds **47**, with **three copies of chromosome 21**.

noteBlocks.prompt: A baby has Down's syndrome. This time the extra chromosome came from the sperm, and the egg held 23 chromosomes. How many chromosomes did the sperm hold?

noteBlocks.alt: A Punnett square for haemophilia. The mother is a carrier: her eggs carry X with the normal allele H or X with the haemophilia allele h, down the side. The father is unaffected: his sperm carry X with the normal allele H or Y, across the top. The four boxes are XH XH, girl, unaffected; XH Y, boy, unaffected; XH Xh, girl, carrier; Xh Y, boy with haemophilia. One child in four has haemophilia, and it is a boy.

noteBlocks.md:
**Higher tier.** Haemophilia stops blood clotting properly. Its allele is carried on the **X chromosome**, and the Y carries no copy. Write the normal allele as $X^{H}$ and the haemophilia allele as $X^{h}$.

A **female** with $X^{H}X^{h}$ is a **carrier**: the normal allele on her other X hides it. A **male** has only one X, so $X^{h}Y$ has haemophilia.

A son gets his **X from his mother** and his **Y from his father**. So a father never passes haemophilia to a son, and every daughter of an affected father receives his haemophilia allele.

noteBlocks.explain: His father gives him the Y. The allele rides only on the X, and a father's X goes to his daughters.

noteBlocks.md:
**Genetic screening** tests people for a harmful allele or a chromosome abnormality. Two tests can be offered in pregnancy.

**Amniocentesis:** a needle is passed through the abdomen into the uterus, a little **amniotic fluid** is drawn off, and the **foetal cells** in it are checked. The answer is certain, but the test is done later in pregnancy and carries a small risk of **miscarriage**.

A **blood test** on the mother can be done earlier and carries no risk to the pregnancy, but it gives only a **chance**, not a certain answer.

data.caption: The gametes of each parent are already written in. Fill in the four empty boxes.

parts.stem:
The Punnett square shows the gametes of a mother and a father.
Complete the four boxes to show the sex chromosomes of their possible children.

scheme.for: the two boxes under the father's X gamete: XX and XX
the two boxes under the father's Y gamete: XY and XY
all four boxes correct

parts.stem: Name the condition on the specification that is caused by a recessive allele, so that a person needs two copies of the allele to have it.

scheme.for: cystic fibrosis

accepted: Huntington's disease
it is Huntington's disease

parts.workedSolution: Huntington's disease.

parts.workedSolution: Homozygous recessive: both alleles are the recessive one.

parts.stem:

parts.workedSolution: Homozygous dominant or heterozygous: one copy of the dominant allele is enough, so both genotypes give Huntington's disease.

parts.stem:
This person developed from a fertilised egg. The sperm cell held 23 chromosomes, and the extra chromosome came from the egg cell.

parts.stem: What is meant by a carrier of cystic fibrosis?

any: receives the recessive allele from both
one recessive allele from each parent
a recessive allele from each parent

the child receives a recessive allele from each parent and so has two of them

hints: A carrier has one allele of each kind, one on each X.

parts.stem:
Which genotype does a man with haemophilia have?
Circle the correct answer.

options.text: $X^{h}Y$ (the haemophilia allele on his one X)

parts.stem:
In one family, the father has haemophilia and the mother has two normal alleles.

accepted: a son receives his father's Y chromosome, and the Y chromosome does not carry the haemophilia allele

any: father gives his son a y
no haemophilia allele on the y
allele is carried on the x

the Y chromosome does not carry the haemophilia allele (it is carried on the X)

hints: Which sex chromosome does a father give to a son?

commonErrors.feedback: A father gives his X to his daughters and his Y to his sons. That is exactly why a son never gets his father's haemophilia allele.

parts.stem:
In that family, what will every daughter be?

A daughter always receives her father's X, and his X carries the haemophilia allele.

hints: Which sex chromosome does a father give to every daughter?

parts.stem:

Individual 3 on the pedigree has cystic fibrosis.

Circle the correct answer.

options.feedback: The condition is recessive, so it only shows when both alleles are the recessive one.

accepted: a male with cystic fibrosis
male who has cystic fibrosis

parts.stem:
Individuals 1 and 2 have another child.
Calculate the percentage chance that the child has cystic fibrosis.

scheme.for: both parents are Ff, so the boxes are FF, Ff, Ff, ff

hints: Write both parents' genotypes, then the four boxes.
parts.workedSolution: Both parents are Ff, so the boxes are FF, Ff, Ff, ff. One in four is ff, so 25%.

Calculate the percentage of the babies born with Down's syndrome.
Give your answer to two decimal places.
hints: Part over whole, then × 100.

commonErrors.feedback: The division is upside down: that is the births divided by the babies with Down's syndrome. The part goes on top of the whole.

context.setting: The arguments for and against genetic screening

parts.stem:
Genetic screening can show whether a baby has an inherited condition before it is born.
Describe the tests that can be used and evaluate the ethical issues that genetic screening raises.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: a blood test takes a sample of the mother's blood, can be done early and carries no risk to the pregnancy, but gives only a chance
amniocentesis uses a needle to take amniotic fluid containing foetal cells, and gives a certain answer
amniocentesis carries a small risk of miscarriage, which has to be weighed against the value of knowing
someone has to decide who is tested: the parents, doctors or the health service
a diagnosis leaves the parents with a hard decision, including whether to continue the pregnancy
a carrier who is tested faces a dilemma: what to do with the result, and whether to tell relatives who may also carry it
if genetic information reaches wider society, insurance companies or employers might use it unfairly

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: An answer that lists practical objections, such as cost, waiting times or distance, where the question asks about ethics reaches few of the indicative points. So does one that describes only one test. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement, and a point contradicted later in the answer is not counted.

hints: Describe both tests first, with one fact about each, then move on to the decisions people have to make.
An ethical point is about right and wrong, or about who is entitled to decide or to know.
parts.workedSolution: Two kinds of test can be offered. A blood test takes a sample of the mother's blood. It can be done early in the pregnancy and carries no risk to the pregnancy, but it gives only a chance, not a certain answer. Amniocentesis uses a needle to take a little of the amniotic fluid, which contains cells from the foetus, and it gives a certain answer. However, it is done later and carries a small risk of miscarriage, which has to be weighed against the value of knowing. The ethical issues begin with who decides who is tested: the parents, the doctors or the health service. If a condition is found, the parents face a difficult decision, including whether to continue the pregnancy, and people disagree deeply about what is right. A carrier who is tested faces a dilemma too: what to do with the result, and whether to tell relatives who may also carry the allele. Finally, if genetic information reaches wider society, insurance companies or employers might use it unfairly, for example to refuse cover or a job.

commonErrors.feedback: Cost and waiting are practical objections. An ethical discussion is about who decides, what the parents should do with the result, and who is entitled to know.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'A sperm cell with 23 chromosomes fertilises an egg cell, and the baby has Down's syndrome because of an extra chromosome in the egg. How many chromosomes did the egg cell hold? [1]'
Her working:
studentWorking: a body cell of someone with Down's syndrome holds 47 chromosomes
an egg always holds 23, so the egg held 23
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 falls back on the usual gamete number, but this egg was not usual: it is where the extra chromosome came from. The fertilised egg holds 47 and the sperm brought 23, so the egg held 47 − 23 = 24.
correction: a body cell of someone with Down's syndrome holds 47 chromosomes
findTheMistake.feedback: No mark, because the one mark was the number. The check that catches it: 23 + 23 makes 46, not 47, so one of the two gametes must have held an extra chromosome.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciarán is asked: 'List every genotype that gives a person Huntington's disease. [2]'
His answer:
studentWorking: Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele, H
a person needs two copies of the allele to have the condition
so the genotype must be homozygous dominant, HH
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 uses the rule for a recessive allele. A dominant allele shows whenever it is present, so one copy is enough: a heterozygous person, Hh, has Huntington's disease too, and line 3 misses that genotype.
correction: Huntington's disease is caused by a dominant allele, H
one copy of a dominant allele is enough to have the condition
so the genotype can be homozygous dominant, HH, or heterozygous, Hh
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of the two, for the homozygous dominant genotype. The check is in the word itself: a dominant allele is the one that shows when only one copy is present.

prompts.prompt: A human female has the sex chromosomes ___ and a human male has ___.
prompts.answer: A human female has the sex chromosomes XX and a human male has XY.

prompts.prompt: Which sex chromosomes are in a germ cell in a man's testis, and which in one sperm cell?
prompts.answer: An X and a Y in a germ cell; an X or a Y in each sperm cell, because meiosis gives each sperm one of the pair.

prompts.prompt: What ratio of boys to girls does the sex-determination square give, and why is it the same for every pregnancy?
prompts.answer: 1 : 1, a 50% chance either way, because half the father's sperm carry a Y every time.

prompts.prompt: Give the cause of each of the four conditions CCEA names.
prompts.answer: Cystic fibrosis: a recessive allele. Huntington's disease: a dominant allele. Down's syndrome: an extra copy of chromosome 21. Haemophilia (Higher): a recessive allele carried on the X chromosome.

prompts.prompt: A person with Down's syndrome has ___ chromosomes in each body cell, because there are ___ copies of chromosome 21.
prompts.answer: A person with Down's syndrome has 47 chromosomes in each body cell, because there are 3 copies of chromosome 21.

prompts.prompt: Which genotypes can a person with Huntington's disease have?
prompts.answer: Homozygous dominant or heterozygous: one copy of the dominant allele is enough.

prompts.prompt: What is a carrier of cystic fibrosis, and what is the chance that two carriers have a child with it?
prompts.answer: Someone with one copy of the recessive allele who does not have the condition. Two carriers have a 25% chance of an affected child.
keyWords: one copy of the recessive allele

prompts.prompt: Higher tier. Why does haemophilia affect far more males than females?
prompts.answer: A male has one X chromosome, so one haemophilia allele is enough; a female with one has a normal allele on her other X and is only a carrier.

prompts.prompt: Describe how amniocentesis is carried out, in three steps.
prompts.answer: A needle is pushed into the uterus; a sample of amniotic fluid is taken; the foetal cells in it are tested.

prompts.prompt: Name the four ethical issues of genetic screening that the specification lists.
prompts.answer: Who decides who is tested; the risks of amniocentesis against the benefits of a blood test; the dilemma for a carrier after a diagnosis; and making genetic information available to wider society, such as insurance companies.
